label: City · Year 2 lab
title: Building an ECG amplifier one stage at a time
name: ECG biopotential amplifier
role: Chose component values, built and tested the circuit
institution: City, University of London · EE2703 Biomedical Instrumentation
tools: TL084 and INA121 amplifiers, breadboard prototyping, Agilent InfiniiVision oscilloscope, signal generator, multimeter
alt: Oscilloscope showing the amplified cardiac test waveform from the finished ECG amplifier
summary: A breadboard ECG amplifier, built up from a single op-amp to an instrumentation amplifier and band-pass filter, with every stage measured against its design value.
takeaway: I built the ECG signal chain one block at a time and measured each one. Moving from a discrete differential amplifier to an INA121 instrumentation amplifier raised common-mode rejection from 32.6 dB to 59.0 dB, and the finished filter passed roughly 0.62–21 Hz against a 0.4–20 Hz design.

sections.title: Why an ECG needs its own amplifier
paragraphs: The heart's electrical signal reaches the skin at only a few millivolts, and it shares the electrodes with mains interference, movement and breathing artefacts. A useful ECG front end has to amplify the small difference between two electrodes, reject what both electrodes see in common, and keep only the frequency band where the cardiac signal lives.

The lab series built that chain in order. Each stage was wired on a breadboard, powered from a split ±15 V supply, driven from a signal generator and judged on an oscilloscope, so the effect of every block could be seen before the next one was added.
steps: Inverting TL084 stage designed for a gain of 10.
Differential amplifier designed for a gain of 18.
INA121 instrumentation amplifier set to a gain of 99 with one 510 Ω resistor.
Second-order Butterworth high-pass (0.4 Hz) and low-pass (20 Hz) stages.
A simulated cardiac waveform passed through the complete chain.

sections.title: Design values against measurements
paragraphs: Every stage was compared with the value it was designed for. Gains came in 4–7% below design at every stage. The clearest difference was in common-mode rejection, where the INA121 did about 26 dB better than the discrete differential amplifier.

table.caption: Measured performance of each stage (voltage ratios unless stated)
rows: Gain 16.86 at 50 Hz, common-mode gain 0.396, CMRR 32.6 dB
Gain 92.5 at 50 Hz, common-mode gain 0.104, CMRR 59.0 dB
About 0.62–21 Hz at the −3 dB points (interpolated)

after: The instrumentation amplifier performed best largely because it needed fewer external parts. One gain resistor replaced several resistor pairs whose tolerances otherwise stack up and unbalance the inputs, which is the likeliest reason for the discrete differential amplifier's weaker common-mode rejection.

sections.title: Shaping the ECG band
paragraphs: The low-pass stage used 100 nF capacitors and 80 kΩ resistors, with a stated gain of 1.57. It passed 1 Hz with a gain of 1.25, fell to 0.73 at 20 Hz and dropped to 0.17 at 1 kHz. The report compared the 20 Hz reading with 0.707, but for a stage with a pass-band gain above 1 the −3 dB level is higher, so this stage's cut-off was probably below 20 Hz.

The high-pass stage used 680 nF capacitors and 581.5 kΩ resistors, chosen from the parts available. It attenuated 0.3 Hz as intended, but its gain above the cut-off recovered only to 0.87, lower than designed. Combined, the band-pass response peaked at about 8.9 dB between 5 and 10 Hz.

figure.alt: Line chart of measured gain in decibels against frequency from 0.1 Hz to 100 Hz, peaking near 9 dB between 5 and 10 Hz
figure.caption: Measured frequency response of the complete band-pass stage, from the lab report. Frequencies are plotted at even spacing, not on a log scale.

sections.title: Where the noise came from
paragraphs: The report traced most of the remaining error to mismatched resistor values, component tolerance and the lab environment: mains-powered equipment, nearby devices and loose breadboard wiring. Battery power or isolation, a notch filter at the mains frequency and secure connections were the suggested remedies.

It also asked what would change to record muscle activity instead. EMG occupies a much wider band than ECG, so the filter cut-offs, interference filtering and electrodes would all need to change. A year later I worked with EMG directly, in my robotic-arm dissertation.

figure.alt: Breadboard with the amplifier and filter circuit connected to the lab power and signal terminals
figure.caption: The breadboard build connected to the lab power and signal terminals.

sections.title: Reading it back two years later
paragraphs: The circuit work holds up; the report shows how much my writing has changed since. It walks through the lab procedure step by step, takes a single reading at each setting and applies a component tolerance only once, to the filter cut-offs, rather than predicting a spread for each stage. Some voltage ratios are labelled as decibels, and the low-pass cut-off is judged against the wrong reference level.

Today I would repeat each measurement, predict the expected spread from component tolerances before testing, and separate method from findings. My later reports, such as the fNIRS dissertation and the surgical-workflow study, follow that structure.

quiz.question: How much better did the instrumentation amplifier reject common-mode noise?
quiz.reveal: About 20×. Common-mode rejection rose from 32.6 dB to 59.0 dB.

label: City · Year 2 team project
title: Checking two heart-rate sensors against each other
name: Heart-rate sensor redundancy monitor
role: Designed and built the full system for a four-person team
institution: City, University of London · EE2600 Digital Design · Group B5
tools: Logisim, D and JK flip-flops, gate-level adders, comparators, multiplexers and registers
alt: Block diagram: ECG and pulse-oximeter inputs feed a redundancy monitor, then a threshold comparator, then green, amber and red alarm lights
summary: A gate-level digital system that reads heart-rate values from an ECG and a pulse oximeter, measures how far they disagree and escalates an alarm from green to amber to red as threshold exceedances accumulate.
takeaway: I designed and built the whole circuit for our group, from the input shift registers to the alarm logic, and tested each block against expected outputs. The adder-subtractor, comparators, counters and registers were built from logic gates and flip-flops rather than Logisim's ready-made arithmetic components.

sections.title: Two sensors, one question
paragraphs: An ECG measures the heart's electrical activity directly. A pulse oximeter estimates heart rate indirectly, from changes in light absorption as blood pulses through tissue. When both are attached to a patient, they should agree. A persistent disagreement suggests one of them is failing.

The system compares the two readings and counts how often the difference exceeds a tolerance, escalating the alert step by step rather than jumping straight to red on a single reading. It was designed and tested in Logisim simulation with chosen test inputs, not connected to physical sensors.

sections.title: How the system is organised
paragraphs: The design follows the signal from serial input to alarm. A central redundancy monitor sits in the middle and does the comparison.
steps: Each sensor's 8-bit value shifts in serially through eight D flip-flops on a shared clock.
A three-flip-flop JK counter waits for all eight bits before enabling the subtractor.
A gate-level two's-complement adder-subtractor computes the difference between the readings.
An 8-bit comparator checks the difference against the error threshold.
A parallel register captures the difference whenever it reaches the threshold.
A counter steps the LEDs from green to amber to red as exceedances repeat.

figure.alt: Full Logisim circuit connecting shift registers, subtractor, comparator, register and LED alarm
figure.caption: The complete Logisim circuit, from the group report. Red wires show Logisim's error state in the captured screenshot.

sections.title: Design choices
paragraphs: Most decisions traded generality for fewer control signals and blocks that could be verified one at a time.

table.caption: Key design decisions and the reasoning behind them
rows: One data input and only a reset to manage; a natural fit for serial-to-parallel conversion
Three flip-flops give the eight states needed, with few extra gates
Two's complement with XOR gates as controlled inverters
Comparator and multiplexer swap the inputs
The larger reading is always the one subtracted from, so the difference is never negative
Most-significant bits take priority, and each level can be checked separately

figure.alt: Logisim schematic of the JK flip-flop alarm counter driving green, yellow and red outputs
figure.caption: Alarm generation: a JK counter selects which LEDs are lit.

sections.title: Testing each block
paragraphs: Each block was probed in simulation against expected outputs before the system was assembled.

table.caption: Block-level tests reported in the group report
rows: Eight clock cycles of serial input
Output shifted one bit per cycle exactly as expected
Both gave 11111111, so no negative values
Green, then amber, then red, staying red

after: All the tests passed, but they were functional checks with a handful of chosen inputs rather than exhaustive verification.

sections.title: What I would add now
paragraphs: The tests show that each block works, but not where it might fail. I would now add boundary cases such as readings exactly at the threshold, timing diagrams showing when the enable signal fires, and a clear link from each requirement to the test that checks it.

I would also state the tolerance in beats per minute and explain where it came from. That clinical framing, which turns a logic exercise into a safety check, is what I later worked on directly in the CE-marking assessment and the fNIRS dissertation.

quiz.question: Flip the inputs and try each gate. Which one lights up only when A and B disagree?
quiz.reveal: XOR, short for exclusive OR: it outputs 1 only when its inputs differ. My heart monitor asked the same of two 8-bit heart-rate readings, using XOR gates inside a gate-level subtractor to measure how far the ECG and pulse oximeter disagreed.

title: Making implant follow-up easier to collect and review
name: REDCap orthopaedic outcome tracking
tools: REDCap, questionnaire design, calculated fields, survey distribution, team training
alt: REDCap research data capture platform logo
summary: A structured post-operative feedback workflow for patient-specific implants, organising anatomy-specific assessments and automated survey follow-up.
takeaway: I built questionnaires, organised the clinical data structure, configured survey distribution and trained the R&D team. The result was a repeatable workflow for reviewing implant feedback.

sections.title: The operational problem
paragraphs: At KOLN 3D, a manufacturer of metallic surgical implants, post-operative feedback had to connect the implant, the operation and the patient's recovery. A general feedback question could not capture the different functional concerns of a hip, an elbow or an orbital procedure.

The project translated that need into a REDCap workflow for structured patient and surgeon feedback. My work covered questionnaire implementation, anatomy-specific organisation, automated email distribution and training the R&D team to manage the process.

sections.title: Start with the operation, then the assessment
paragraphs: The form began with patient-specific implant details, serial number, operation location and date, and follow-up date. A surgical-region selection then organised the relevant clinical assessment. Skull procedures included an additional region choice.

The assessment structure combined named orthopaedic instruments with custom post-operative sections. Keeping that distinction visible matters: implementing questions in REDCap does not itself validate a questionnaire, a calculated field or a new scoring interpretation.

table.caption: Assessment coverage in the project materials
rows: Named instrument implemented as a digital form
Named instrument implemented as a digital form
Named instrument implemented as a digital form
Named instrument implemented as a digital form
Named instrument implemented as a digital form

after: Depending on the region, questions captured pain, stability, motion, walking support, daily activities or procedure-specific symptoms. Calculated fields gave each assessment a consistent place in the record, alongside the underlying responses.

sections.title: The feedback workflow
steps: Associate the implant and operation with the follow-up.
Distribute surveys and capture structured responses.
Store the assessment output alongside its source answers.
Make the feedback available to the R&D team.
paragraphs: I recreated the question and response structures in REDCap and configured automated email workflows to support repeatable survey distribution. Organising the records consistently made it easier to follow the same implant through successive feedback points.
Training was part of delivery. The R&D team needed to understand how to manage the surveys, monitor responses and interpret the collection workflow after the implementation work ended.

sections.title: Making sense of the scores
paragraphs: I also prepared a short interpretation reference to accompany the calculated outputs. This mapped each assessment to its own score bands, rather than assuming that the same numeric value meant the same thing across all instruments.

The supplied scoring notes make that need clear: different instruments use different boundaries and category labels. Custom orbital, TMJ and lung-function sections were explicitly marked as self-implemented. They should be understood as project-specific collection tools, with clinical review required before any decision-making use.
The portfolio describes the structure and engineering work. It does not provide a clinical calculator or reproduce completed patient records.

sections.title: What the work delivered
paragraphs: The deliverable was a structured, repeatable way to collect post-operative feedback and organise it for review. It brought the survey, scoring fields and operational handover into one workflow.
The project materials demonstrate the form structure and interpretation notes. They do not quantify response-rate improvements, time saved or improved patient outcomes, so those are not claimed here.

The wider internship also included production-planning automation with Excel VBA and Power Automate, an internal CNC mould guide supporting six-degree-of-freedom drilling setup, and 3D-printed display models for commercial use.

sections.title: What this taught me about clinical software
paragraphs: The hard part was translating a clinical process into something consistent enough to operate repeatedly. That meant asking what each field represented, when a question was relevant and who would use the result.

A useful next iteration would make formula verification, instrument-version tracking and missing-response handling explicit, then evaluate the workflow against agreed operational measures. That would allow usability and efficiency claims to be backed by evidence.

sourceNote: Based on the blank 11-page REDCap form exported in June 2024, the accompanying score-interpretation notes and the original portfolio's internship record. The internal form is described here without publishing its original export.

quiz.reveal: No. Each instrument has its own score bands, so I mapped every assessment separately.

title: Turning muscle activity into a working grasp
name: Low-cost EMG-controlled robotic arm
institution: City St George's, University of London
tools: Arduino Nano, C++, analogue EMG electronics, SolidWorks, Fusion 360, FDM 3D printing
alt: CAD visualisation of the robotic hand and forearm design
summary: An Arduino-controlled, tendon-driven hand and wrist, bringing surface EMG sensing, analogue electronics and 3D-printed mechanics into one prototype.
takeaway: I developed a low-cost hand-and-wrist prototype around a sub-£100 parts budget. The work centred on integrating a noisy biological input with a simple, maintainable mechanical system.

sections.title: The design brief
paragraphs: My undergraduate dissertation investigated a low-cost EMG-controlled prosthetic-arm concept using desktop 3D printing and Arduino-compatible electronics. The target was basic grasping within a parts budget below £100, excluding in-house printing labour.

The final scope was a hand and wrist, without an articulated elbow. It was an engineering proof of concept, rather than a patient-ready prosthesis. I worked across sensing, electronics, firmware, CAD, assembly and initial evaluation under the supervision of Dr James May.

sections.title: From a muscle signal to a command
paragraphs: Surface electrodes captured muscle activity. Because the small, rapidly changing signal could not directly drive a motor, the analogue front end amplified it, rectified it and filtered it into an envelope related to contraction intensity. A DC offset made that signal compatible with the Arduino's input range.

The design used an AD8226 instrumentation amplifier and TL084 stages for rectification and filtering. The important system-level choice was to condition the biological signal before applying a deliberately simple control rule.
steps: Amplification, rectification and filtering produce an envelope.
Arduino estimates activity relative to a changing baseline.
Servo pulleys pull the tendons to close the hand.
after: The firmware used a running root-mean-square estimate and an adaptive baseline. Separate thresholds for closing and opening introduced hysteresis, reducing repeated switching near a single threshold. A short post-command interval gave the servos time to respond.
This was binary open/close control, not independent finger classification or proportional grip control. That limit kept the algorithm understandable and the hardware cost manageable.

sections.title: Mechanical iteration
paragraphs: The hand used PLA finger segments and a tendon-and-pulley transmission driven by three hobby servos. Fishing line provided a low-cost tendon material, while the forearm housed the motors, electronics and wiring.

table.caption: Design changes made to simplify assembly and improve consistency
rows: Segments could skew under tendon tension
Reinforced hinge geometry, pins and centred tendon channels
Wall flex and friction around tendon exits
Thicker local geometry and an accessible palm lid
A geared concept introduced backlash and print-tolerance demands
A simpler ball-and-socket direction with tendon anchors
Fragile segmented clips and trapped wiring
A shell with removable access panels and internal mounting features

after: Repair access mattered as much as initial assembly. The palm lid exposed tendon adjustment points; removable forearm panels made the servos and electronics accessible. Standardising finger geometry also reduced the number of unique replacement parts.
The trade-off was coupled movement. Sharing actuators and tendon routes lowered cost and complexity, while limiting fine dexterity and making slack and friction central performance constraints.

sections.title: Keeping sensing and actuation stable
paragraphs: Servo current demand and analogue signal quality had to be considered together. The architecture separated the EMG supply from the servo power rails, with a common grounding arrangement and attention to routing noisy power wiring away from the sensing path.

The integration work involved electrode placement, baseline calibration, mechanical tendon tension and power stability. A threshold that worked well in one setup could become unreliable when contact shifted or the mechanical load changed.
Those interactions were the main lesson of the build: a clean control diagram does not remove the need to test the complete physical system.

sections.title: Initial evaluation
paragraphs: The presentation summary reports approximately £91 in parts and around 6 N of combined fingertip force from simple scale measurements. These are prototype-level observations, not independent product benchmarks.

table.caption: Reported fingertip measurements from the presentation summary

after: A short timing test reported five values between 264 and 288 ms, averaging approximately 275 ms. The summary describes the measurement endpoints inconsistently, so this should be read as an indicative control-timing observation rather than a verified muscle-to-motion latency.

The control test was also too small for a dependable accuracy claim. Its stated percentage does not reconcile with the listed event counts. A larger, consistently labelled trial is needed before reporting control accuracy as a performance result.

These limitations do not erase the integration work; they define the next evaluation task. Mechanical force, complete movement time, missed commands and unintended commands need separate, repeatable protocols.

sections.title: What I would improve next
paragraphs: My first priorities would be reducing tendon friction and slack, improving repeatability of electrode placement, and checking the power system under realistic loads. Durability and maintenance would need longer tests than the initial demonstration.

A better controller could use a shorter, carefully evaluated processing window and an additional EMG channel. Proportional grip or multiple gesture classes would then need to justify their added sensing, calibration and computational demands.

Before any clinical use, the design would require formal safety work, appropriate user studies, comfort and socket-fit evaluation, and robust long-term testing. The project established a platform for investigating those questions, not their answers.

quiz.question: What is the most common signal used to control a powered prosthetic arm?
quiz.reveal: Muscle signals (EMG). Electrodes on the skin pick up the electrical activity of muscles as they contract. My hand did the same: it amplified and smoothed that signal into an open or close command, for about £91 in parts.

label: UCL · MSc coursework
title: Does knowing the surgical timeline help a model find the tools?
name: Surgical workflow timing with CNN-LSTM
institution: UCL · MPHY0043 AI for Surgery and Intervention
tools: Python, ResNet-18 (ImageNet-pretrained), LSTM, AdamW, Cholec80, video-level paired bootstrap
alt: Diagram of the CNN-LSTM model predicting remaining phase time and future phase timings from video frames
summary: A two-part study on laparoscopic surgery video: predicting how long each surgical phase has left, then testing whether those predictions help a model detect which tools are in use.
takeaway: A 60-second history predicted the end of the current phase at least as well as 120 seconds (mean absolute error 216 s against 263 s, one training run each). Adding the predicted timing raised tool-detection mAP from 0.910 to 0.918, but a paired bootstrap across the 10 test videos showed the gain was not statistically significant (p = 0.11).

sections.title: The question
paragraphs: Most gallbladder removals are performed laparoscopically, so every operation leaves a full video record. Models that understand where a procedure is in its workflow could support operating-theatre coordination and act as a second pair of eyes during surgery.

The coursework set two connected tasks on the Cholec80 dataset of 80 annotated procedures. First, does a longer video history improve predictions of when the current phase will end? Second, can those timing predictions act as context that makes a tool detector more reliable?

sections.title: One backbone, two tasks
paragraphs: Video was downsampled from 25 to 1 frame per second. An ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 extracted features from each frame, and a one-directional LSTM modelled their sequence, so predictions used only past and present frames, as a live system would. A small head predicted 14 values: the start and end of each of seven phases.

Times were log-transformed to compress long durations. A masked, weighted loss gave the end of the current phase four times the weight of future phases, reflecting its clinical relevance. The backbone was frozen for the first epochs and then fine-tuned at a lower learning rate.

figure.alt: Side-by-side diagrams of a visual-only tool classifier and a time-aware classifier that concatenates predicted timing features
figure.caption: Task B compared a visual-only tool detector with one that also receives the predicted timings. Everything else was kept identical.

sections.title: Results
paragraphs: All numbers in the table are from the 10 held-out test videos.
after: The longer window did not help. Frames from two minutes earlier probably say little about the current phase, and a shorter window is also cheaper to run in real time.

Timing helped most for bipolar forceps (AP 0.849 to 0.907), with smaller gains for scissors, irrigator and specimen bag. The grasper and hook, used across many phases, changed little, but the clipper fell from 0.994 to 0.966, so the benefit was not uniform even among phase-specific tools. Timing behaves as a weak prior rather than a rule.

figure.alt: Bar chart of mAP for baseline and time-aware models on validation and test splits
figure.caption: mAP for the baseline and time-aware models on validation and test videos. The axis is truncated near 0.89, which makes the gap look larger than it is.

sections.title: Is the improvement real?
paragraphs: Frames from the same video are correlated, so I tested the difference with a paired bootstrap that resampled whole videos 2,000 times. The mAP gain averaged +0.009 with a 95% interval of −0.001 to +0.018 (p = 0.11), so it was not significant. Micro-F1 at a fixed 0.5 threshold decreased significantly in the bootstrap.

The headline table and the bootstrap point in different directions for Micro-F1, and the report does not reconcile them. The safest reading is that timing slightly improved how frames were ranked but did not reliably improve thresholded decisions. Each configuration was also trained only once.

sections.title: Limits and next steps
paragraphs: The test set's tool-detection mAP is numerically higher than the roughly 81% reported for EndoNet, but the data splits and training setups differ, so this is not a like-for-like comparison.

Surgeons work at different paces, so a model trained on absolute seconds will under- or over-estimate for slow and fast cases. The next steps would be to predict relative progress through each phase, output uncertainty so downstream models can treat timing as a soft hint, and report results separately for fast, typical and slow procedures. The timing features fed into the tool detector during training were also predicted on videos the timing model had already seen.

quiz.question: Can a neural network watch keyhole surgery and predict how long the current step has left?
quiz.reveal: Roughly. Watching the last 60 seconds of video, my model was off by about 3.6 minutes on average (216 s) and within a minute 29% of the time. Giving it twice as much history did not help (263 s).

title: OsteoTrack: a path from device concept to clinical use
name: OsteoTrack bone-healing monitoring
tools: Clinical literature, competitor research, IP research, commercial planning, launch-page design
summary: A non-invasive fracture-monitoring proposal, connecting vibration sensing with a realistic plan for evidence, adoption and funding.
takeaway: My contribution connected the device's technical premise to its identity, clinical positioning and funding pathway. OsteoTrack remained an academic concept, with validation and deployment proposed as future stages.

sections.title: The follow-up problem
paragraphs: Our group explored how a non-invasive device might support follow-up after a fracture. The clinical motivation was to observe healing over time and identify patients who might need further assessment, without treating every follow-up as an isolated measurement.

We compared bone-assessment approaches including DEXA, CT, MRI, ultrasound, implant-based sensing and vibration-based monitoring. The concept we developed used an external vibration source and accelerometers to track changes in the limb's mechanical response.

The intended setting was a community or clinical point of care. A clinician would review longitudinal measurements and decide whether a patient needed fracture-clinic review or imaging. This was a proposal for decision support, with clinical effectiveness still to be established.

sections.title: How the proposed device worked
paragraphs: The team's mechanical concept combined an inflatable cuff, a vibration motor with a contact disc, and two accelerometers on adjustable mounting strips. The adjustable geometry was intended to accommodate different patients and maintain consistent contact.

A controlled frequency sweep would produce a measured response spectrum. Repeated visits would build a patient-specific trajectory. The proposed software would compare this trajectory with labelled clinical data to support assessment of non-union risk.

figure.alt: Two annotated CAD views of the proposed cuff assembly, with and without the motor housing
figure.caption: Group D concept drawings: adjustable accelerometer positions, cuff attachment and the motor/contact-disc assembly. This is a proposed design, not a clinically validated device.

steps: Fit the cuff and align the sensing points.
Apply a controlled vibration sweep and record the response.
Track the spectrum against earlier visits.
Present the trend to a clinician for assessment.
after: The group report explored cross-spectrum features and a supervised model trained on future clinical-trial data. Patient-labelled training data, repeatability testing and clinical validation were dependencies, rather than completed capabilities.

sections.title: My contribution
paragraphs: As Communications and Fundraising Officer, I initially expected to concentrate on presentation and funding sources. The work quickly became more technical: explaining a medical-device venture credibly required understanding its mechanism, evidence and place in the clinical workflow.

subsections.title: Identity and digital presence
subsections.text: I worked with the Chief Designer and Market Researcher on the OsteoTrack logo, brand identity and launch page. The aim was to present an orthopaedic monitoring platform in a professional, recognisable way, consistent with its early stage of development.

subsections.title: Clinical and commercial positioning
subsections.text: I helped distinguish the person benefiting from the device from the organisation buying it. Patients were the intended beneficiaries, while clinicians, fracture-clinic leads and procurement teams would influence adoption. That distinction shaped the communication strategy.

subsections.title: Intellectual property and funding
subsections.text: I researched relevant intellectual property, early-stage startup planning and fundraising routes. A preliminary patent review raised questions for a future freedom-to-operate assessment; it did not establish freedom to operate or secure patent protection.

sections.title: A staged route to adoption
paragraphs: I helped frame the venture around milestones that could reduce technical and commercial uncertainty. Early communication would support prototype refinement and pilot engagement, then grow with the quality of the clinical evidence.

The group considered private orthopaedic clinics as an initial route for feedback, with NHS adoption as a longer-term objective. Conference presentations, professional engagement and clinical white papers were proposed channels for reaching the people who would evaluate the device.

table.caption: The proposed funding sequence
rows: Prototype refinement, IP review and initial repeatability
Technical evidence and credible clinical partners
Quality processes and a clinical validation plan
Stronger evidence of utility and adoption
Seed investment or debt where appropriate

after: The report explored a per-patient pricing model and longer-term financial projections. These were planning assumptions, not sales, funding secured or demonstrated NHS savings. I treated grants and accelerators as routes to investigate against the venture's stage, rather than promises of available capital.

sections.title: A technical idea still has to fit the brief
paragraphs: I questioned how readily vibration-based evidence from modelled bones would translate into measurements in patients. During competitor research, I explored whether a resonance approach used for implants could inform long-bone assessment, potentially alongside fixation plates.

The group decided that an implant-linked direction would move away from our non-invasive objective and complicate the development pathway. The research still helped us understand the competitive landscape and sharpen the boundaries of the concept.

The team also considered electrical safety, data handling, software governance and clinical investigation requirements. Those topics informed the development plan; they were not claims that the concept had received regulatory approval.

sections.title: What I took from the project
paragraphs: Around fifteen weekly meetings, with clear goals for the next week, helped a multidisciplinary team maintain progress. My own role depended on translating between the technical work and the questions an adopter or funder would ask.

The strongest outcome for me was learning to tie communication to evidence. A professional identity can make an idea understandable, but a convincing medtech proposition also needs a plausible path through validation, procurement and use.

If repeating the project, I would start that work earlier, link technical milestones to communication outputs, and test the proposal with clinicians and procurement stakeholders sooner. I would also keep a regular reflective log to capture how the strategy changed.

label: UCL · Group concept

quiz.question: Who decides whether a hospital adopts a new medical device?
quiz.reveal: Clinicians and procurement teams. Patients benefit, but the clinicians who use a device and the teams who buy it decide. For OsteoTrack, our fracture-monitoring concept, that meant pitching to clinicians, fracture-clinic leads and procurement.

label: UCL · MSc coursework
title: Taking a research robot towards a CE mark
name: EU MDR pathway for a lung-ultrasound robot
institution: UCL · MPHY0046 Medical Robotics and Devices
tools: EU MDR 2017/745, Annex VIII classification rules, EN ISO 13485, ISO 14971, IEC 62304, IEC 62366-1, IEC 60601 series
alt: Diagram of the regulatory route from intended purpose through classification and quality system to notified-body assessment
summary: A regulatory assessment written as the researcher commercialising a published lung-ultrasound scanning robot in the EU: qualification, risk class, quality system, documentation and standards.
takeaway: I argued the robot should be a Class IIa active diagnostic device under Annex VIII Rule 10, with a deliberately narrow intended purpose: clinician-supervised image acquisition, not automated diagnosis. I then mapped the quality system, technical file and standards a notified body would expect to see.

sections.title: The device
paragraphs: The system, published by Tan et al. (2023), is a research-stage robot that scans both sides of the chest with two ultrasound probes. It combines a gantry-style dual-arm platform, structured-light reconstruction of the chest surface, automatic probe-path planning, closed-loop force control and a clinician interface.

The paper reports scans in under four minutes per person, with image quality comparable to manual scanning. Those are the authors' results; my work was to set out what it would take to place the device on the EU market.

sections.title: Defining the claim before the device
paragraphs: Under the MDR, the manufacturer's intended purpose decides whether a product is a medical device and how strictly it is regulated. I defined it conservatively: an active, non-invasive, clinician-supervised imaging device that acquires lung ultrasound images to support bedside assessment of respiratory disease.

It is still a medical device, because acquiring images is part of the diagnostic chain even when a clinician interprets them, and its action is mechanical and acoustic rather than pharmacological. Claiming automated diagnosis would have pulled in a heavier evidence burden the research does not support.

sections.title: Choosing the classification rule
paragraphs: Classification came from testing each candidate rule against the device, not from picking the most familiar one.

table.caption: EU MDR Annex VIII rules considered
rows: Rule 1 is the default for non-invasive devices, but the more specific Rule 10 for active diagnostic devices takes precedence
They cover invasive devices; the probes touch intact skin only
It covers active therapeutic devices; nothing is treated
An active device intended for diagnosis and monitoring
The software drives the hardware rather than standing alone, so it takes the device's class

sections.title: Quality system and technical file
paragraphs: A Class IIa device under Annex IX needs a quality management system; EN ISO 13485:2016 is the accepted framework. For a system that combines robotics, imaging, software and patient contact, it also keeps every subsystem under the same design controls, change control and supplier checks.
steps: Intended purpose, users, patient population and system boundary.
Architecture, drawings, schematics and a risk file covering probe force, positioning errors, electrical safety, EMC, software faults and poor images.
Software tests, bench tests of motion and force control, electrical safety, EMC, usability and image-quality validation.
Clinical evaluation and, if needed, an investigation with protocol and adverse-event procedures.
Supplier control, traceability, complaints, corrective actions, vigilance and the post-market surveillance plan.
after: The supporting standards were ISO 14971 for risk management, IEC 62304 for the software lifecycle, IEC 62366-1 for usability and IEC 60601-1, 60601-1-2 and 60601-2-37 for electrical safety, EMC and ultrasound equipment. Inside the company, the person responsible for regulatory compliance keeps the file current; outside it, a notified body audits it and issues the certificate behind the CE mark.

sections.title: Why this matters for an engineer
paragraphs: A working prototype and a device that can legally be sold are different things. This assessment made that concrete: most of the work lies in evidence, traceability and controlled change, not in the robot itself.
It connects my clinical follow-up work at KOLN 3D and the adoption plan in OsteoTrack. The classification here is my reasoned coursework argument, not a regulatory determination.

sourceNote: The answers follow the module's question template, so the submission is summarised here rather than published. The device is described in Tan et al. (2023), a research paper on a fully automatic dual-probe lung-ultrasound scanning robot.

quiz.question: A medical device that only touches intact skin is called non-invasive. Which EU risk class does it start in?
quiz.reveal: Class I, the lowest. Under EU rules (MDR Annex VIII, Rule 1), non-invasive devices start there, but a more specific rule can move them up. The lung-ultrasound robot I assessed is non-invasive too, yet as an active device used for diagnosis it becomes Class IIa under Rule 10.

label: UCL · MSc coursework
title: Three clinical datasets, three kinds of evidence
name: Surgical data science coursework
tools: Python, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, scikit-image, OpenCV, Jupyter
alt: Overview of the three assignments: ultrasound image quality, surgical skill and CT classification, and ECG beat clustering
summary: Three assignments on clinical data: scoring ultrasound image quality against experts, classifying surgical skill and COVID-19 CT scans, and clustering ECG beats without labels.
takeaway: Across all three I chose methods to fit the data: normality checks before choosing between Welch and Mann–Whitney tests, cross-validated classifiers judged on the error that matters clinically, and label-free clustering scored against the true classes only afterwards. Several results were negative, and I reported them as such.

sections.title: Part 1 · Do image metrics agree with expert scores?
paragraphs: The dataset held transoesophageal echo images from 20 participants, 7 experts and 13 novices, across 10 views. Each image had two manual quality scores and a gold-standard reference. The two manual scores correlated positively in every view, most strongly in View 1.

I compared each image with its reference using structural similarity, mutual information and cosine similarity. Mutual information and cosine similarity differed significantly between experts and novices (p < 0.05, uncorrected across 30 tests) in 2 of 10 views; structural similarity did so in 1. A degree-7 polynomial ridge regression from these metrics to the manual scores reached R² ≈ 0.56 at best. Image misalignment, measured by ECC registration, showed no significant expert–novice difference in any view.
after: With about 20 images per view, those regression fits are in-sample and optimistic. I would now hold out data before reporting them.

sections.title: Part 2 · Classifying surgical skill and COVID-19 CT
paragraphs: Using JIGSAWS robotic suturing data from four expert and four novice surgeons, I extracted 22 motion parameters. Completion time separated the groups most clearly: experts averaged 86.5 ± 14.5 s and novices 141.2 ± 52.9 s. Five features (time, path length and velocity for both instruments) fed three classifiers.

table.caption: Cross-validated skill classification
rows: Fewest novices labelled as experts (4 of 20)
Missed only 1 expert trial, but labelled 6 novices as experts

after: I recommended the random forest: in surgical training, certifying a novice too early is the more dangerous error. The folds held out one trial per surgeon, so these scores do not test performance on unseen surgeons.

On 746 CT images, linear and quadratic discriminant analysis reached 0.71 and 0.58 accuracy, with QDA over-predicting COVID-19. HoG features with an RBF support vector machine reached 0.81. On an unbalanced subset (349 COVID-19, 197 non-COVID), the SVM reached 0.83 unweighted and 0.84 with class weighting, so most of the change came from the altered class mix. Published deep-learning models score higher, but they use far richer training, so the comparison is not like-for-like.

sections.title: Part 3 · Clustering ECG beats without labels
paragraphs: 1,800 heartbeats from three classes (normal, supraventricular ectopic and ventricular ectopic) were described by 83 features. PCA kept over 90% of the variance in far fewer dimensions. The clustering methods never saw the labels; the labels were used only to score them afterwards.
after: The weaker linkage methods collapsed almost every beat into one normal cluster. Supraventricular beats were the hardest class for every method that worked, with at best 455 of 600 grouped correctly (Ward linkage on PCA features), because they overlap with normal beats in feature space. The Gaussian mixture did best overall, probably because it lets clusters take different shapes and spreads.

sections.title: What the three have in common
paragraphs: Each assignment came down to the same habits: check the assumptions before choosing a test, pick the metric that reflects the clinical cost of an error, and say plainly when a method fails. Those habits are also the main difference between this work and my second-year lab reports.

quiz.question: What best separated expert surgeons from novices?
quiz.reveal: Completion time. Experts averaged 86.5 s on the suturing task; novices averaged 141.2 s.

title: What can walking tell us about the brain?
name: fNIRS classification during complex walking
tools: Python, scikit-learn, SciPy, pandas, pytest, SPM outputs
alt: Experimental walking route with lighting and obstacle conditions
summary: A participant-level machine-learning study of prefrontal responses under different lighting and obstacle conditions, with careful validation of what a small dataset can support.
takeaway: I built and tested a complete analysis pipeline. The best observed model reached 61.9% balanced accuracy, but selection-adjusted testing did not establish performance above chance.

sections.title: The research question
paragraphs: Could prefrontal brain responses recorded during walking distinguish autistic and neurotypical adults? The question moved beyond differences between group averages to ask whether those responses could classify a previously unseen participant.

I analysed an existing UCL PEARL walking-and-lighting dataset. The original experiment varied blue versus yellow illumination, dim versus bright light, and the presence of obstacles. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) provided a portable measure of changes in cortical haemoglobin during these tasks.

My work began with the inherited, first-level SPM outputs. I did not collect the original recordings, repeat raw-signal preprocessing, or refit the original general linear model. My contribution was the secondary analysis: data validation, feature construction, classification, statistical testing and interpretation.

sections.title: From SPM files to comparable features
paragraphs: A file being readable did not mean it was usable. I checked the design matrices, regressor names and stored beta estimates for compatible dimensions, finite values and the required task conditions. Four of the 36 participants had a required task column containing only zeros and were excluded before model fitting.

The final analytical cohort contained 32 participants: 19 neurotypical and 13 autistic. I pooled condition-specific oxygenated-haemoglobin beta estimates from 22 channels into seven predefined prefrontal regions, keeping the inputs compact and anatomically interpretable.

table.caption: Four feature representations, each evaluated with three linear classifiers
rows: Broad averages for yellow walking, blue walking and non-walking events
Four condition differences across seven regions
Global, hemispheric and regional-family summaries of the four contrasts
A focused representation of the lighting-spectrum contrast

after: The four contrasts were blue minus yellow, dim minus bright, obstacle minus no obstacle, and non-walking minus walking. They were constructed without group labels. Expressing differences within each participant also reduced the emphasis on broad participant-level response offsets.

sections.title: Validation was part of the design
paragraphs: I compared shrinkage linear discriminant analysis (LDA), L2-regularised logistic regression and a linear support vector machine. With almost as many predictors as training participants, regularised linear models offered a more defensible starting point than a highly flexible classifier.

The outer validation loop used four stratified folds repeated 25 times. Each of the 100 outer evaluations held out participants entirely. Three-fold inner validation selected hyperparameters using only the outer training set. Standardisation, optional PCA and questionnaire imputation stayed inside the fitted pipelines.
steps: Check the SPM design and required conditions before inclusion.
Aggregate channels into regions and construct fixed feature sets.
Fit preprocessing and choose hyperparameters within training folds.
Score untouched participants using the same splits for all models.
Repeat the full comparison with shuffled participant labels.
after: Comparing 12 configurations creates another opportunity for optimism: one configuration may look best by chance. I ran 1,000 participant-label permutations, repeating the entire nested analysis and retaining the best score across all 12 configurations for each permutation. This produced a selection-aware reference distribution.

sections.title: The result, including its limits
paragraphs: Contrast-based representations performed better descriptively than broad task-context averages. Full-contrast LDA produced the strongest observed result, but the error pattern was uneven: neurotypical specificity was high and autistic recall was low.

table.caption: Full-contrast LDA performance and selection-adjusted inference

figure.alt: Dissertation Figure 4 comparing balanced accuracy, ROC-AUC and MCC across twelve model configurations
figure.caption: Original dissertation Figure 4. Contrast features improved descriptive performance, but the selected result remained statistically uncertain.

after: The configuration-specific p-value for full-contrast LDA was 0.0539. After selection across the 12 configurations, it was 0.2358: 235 of 1,000 shuffled-label runs achieved a best score at least as high as the observed result. The study therefore did not establish a reliable classifier or a clinically useful diagnostic tool.
The repeated evaluations reused the same 32 people. They helped characterise sensitivity to data splits; they did not turn a small cohort into 100 independent validation samples.

sections.title: Looking beyond a single score
paragraphs: I examined participant-level prediction stability to distinguish people who were repeatedly misclassified from people whose predictions changed across splits. Errors were concentrated among a subset of autistic participants, making the overall score an incomplete description of model behaviour.

Adding the Sensory Perception Quotient (SPQ) to the full-contrast features produced small, classifier-dependent changes. It mainly changed the balance between recall and specificity rather than adding a consistent predictive benefit.

PCA provided a useful counterexample to the assumption that preserving variance preserves useful information. It retained a median of five components and 95.2% of total feature variance, yet balanced accuracy fell from 0.6185 to 0.5881. I projected PCA-space classifier coefficients back into the original standardised feature space and numerically checked their reconstructed decision scores.

sections.title: Making the analysis reproducible
paragraphs: The final dissertation reports 87 passing automated tests across seven modules, with two expected questionnaire-merge warnings. Tests covered SPM validation, synthetic ROI calculations, contrast directions, invalid feature tables, nested-validation outputs, participant summaries, questionnaire matching and permutation statistics.

I documented random seeds, software versions, analysis scripts and aggregate outputs. The result is a reproducible research workflow whose assumptions and failure cases can be inspected, even when the scientific answer is inconclusive.

The next useful step is stronger evidence: a larger independent cohort, richer metadata and external validation. More model searching on the same small sample would not resolve the underlying uncertainty.
